summary: The last 4 weeks show a very low and inconsistent training volume — only 8 sessions logged, with chronic sleep deprivation (most nights under 6 hours, several under 5) and persistently low body battery scores dragging recovery well below what's needed for race preparation. With the Half Oceanman 5,000m swim just 21 days away, swimming volume is critically underdone: only three open-water sessions totalling ~4km in the block, all at elevated HR (avg ~160 bpm), suggesting significant aerobic swim fatigue. Cycling base is more present but still modest, and running is entirely absent from the recorded data.
suggestions: Prioritise sleep above all else this week — chronic under-recovery (avg ~340 min/night, body battery frequently under 40) is the single biggest limiter to race-day performance and must be addressed before adding training load.

For the Half Oceanman swim (21 days), shift pool sessions this week to confidence-building continuous sets at 2:30/100m or slower — avoid high-intensity swim work that spikes HR further and adds to accumulated fatigue.
The Wk13 Saturday long ride (19 Sep) is already AI-adjusted to 60km/120 min — honour that cap strictly; pushing to 115km at this recovery deficit and race proximity would be counterproductive.
Drop the Wk14 threshold cycling intervals (24 Sep, 5×5min @ 210–244W) given that race week begins Oct 2 — swap to a Z2 maintenance spin to avoid carrying residual leg fatigue into the Half Oceanman.

Running volume post-Half Oceanman (Oct 4 long run at 21.5km) should be reduced to 12–14km easy given the expected swim race fatigue — arriving fresh for the Treviso 10K (Oct 10) matters more than hitting the planned distance.

proposed_changes.reason: Chronic sleep debt and body battery consistently below 50 make a 20km long run today high-injury-risk with only 21 days to the Half Oceanman swim; a shortened easy run preserves aerobic stimulus without compounding fatigue.

proposed_changes.reason: A 4-hour ride 6 days before the Half Oceanman swim race would leave the athlete carrying fatigue into race week; halving the duration protects freshness while maintaining aerobic feel.

proposed_changes.reason: Five days out from the Half Oceanman, a 21km long run creates unnecessary leg fatigue — a short easy jog keeps the body moving without compromising race-day readiness.

proposed_changes.reason: The day after a 5,000m open-water race, a 21.5km long run is excessive and risks injury going into the Treviso 10K just 6 days later; a short easy run aids recovery while keeping the legs moving.

proposed_changes.reason: Recent open-water swims show avg HR of 160–161 bpm indicating the athlete is working hard to cover even moderate distances; shifting to controlled continuous blocks at a slightly relaxed pace builds confidence and aerobic efficiency for the 5,000m race.
